title: Beige Book — April 23, 2025
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2025-04-23 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Activity was roughly flat. Five Districts saw slight growth, three were relatively unchanged and four reported slight to modest declines. Manufacturing was mixed, with two-thirds of Districts reporting little change or declines. Home sales rose somewhat despite low inventory, and commercial real estate expanded slightly, led by multifamily. Loan demand was flat to modestly higher, energy grew modestly, agriculture was fairly stable and transportation expanded modestly. Nonfinancial services demand deteriorated in several Districts. Outlooks worsened considerably in several Districts. The report was prepared by the Atlanta Fed.

Consumer spending

Non-auto spending fell overall, but most Districts saw moderate to robust vehicle sales and some nondurable sales as buyers rushed ahead of tariff-driven price increases. Leisure and business travel declined, and several Districts reported fewer international visitors.

Labor markets

Employment was little changed to slightly higher: one District reported a modest gain, four slight gains, four no change and three slight declines. Consumer-facing firms hired more slowly than business-to-business firms. The largest headcount losses were in government and government-funded organizations. Many firms paused hiring, with scattered reports of layoff preparations. Labor availability improved, though shifting immigration policy limited supply in some places. Wage growth was modest and slowed in multiple Districts.

Prices

Prices rose everywhere: six Districts called the pace modest and six moderate. Firms expected tariffs to raise input costs, and many suppliers had already announced increases. Firms added tariff surcharges and shortened pricing horizons; most planned to pass costs to customers. Some, especially consumer-facing firms, saw margins compress where demand was weak. Price expectations were elevated.

Notable themes

  • Tariffs: Uncertainty over trade policy was "pervasive across reports."
  • Pull-forward buying: Vehicle purchases ahead of expected tariff price hikes.
  • Government cuts: Federal grant and subsidy cuts, plus lower philanthropic giving, left service gaps at community organizations.
  • Immigration: Shifting policy constrained labor supply in some sectors.

District highlights

  • Boston: Outlook turned more pessimistic over tariffs; IT services revenues grew strongly.
  • New York: Activity contracted modestly; price increases at the upper end of moderate.
  • Philadelphia: Business activity fell modestly.
  • Richmond: Weakness tied to federal staffing and contract spending.
  • St. Louis: Heavy rains hurt neighborhoods, farms and businesses.
  • Minneapolis: Activity and employment declined.
  • Kansas City: Price-growth expectations rose sharply, especially for goods; hiring stalled.
  • Dallas: Growth slowed; outlooks deteriorated amid domestic and trade policy uncertainty.
  • San Francisco: Outlook worsened materially.

Read-through for SPY

  • Stalling growth plus rising price expectations is a stagflation-tinged mix that markets usually dislike.
  • Pull-forward demand may flatter near-term sales but could leave a gap later.
  • Hiring pauses and margin compression at consumer-facing firms were a risk to earnings estimates.
